Q: How can I copy my Git repository from my Windows machine to a Linux machine via a USB drive? A:

The safest option (exclude gitignored and uncommitted files):

git bundle create myreponame.bundle --all is safest, but it won't copy over ignored files in your .gitignore file, such as the local configuration, IDE configuration, secrets, data, etc. It won't copy any uncommitted changes or files either.

An alternative option (include gitignored and uncommitted files):

I recently migrated Git repositories from Windows to Linux (Ubuntu). This is the process I used to migrate dozens of Git repositories which had lots of data, secrets, etc. that were ignored via .gitignore or recent code changes that weren't committed yet, but I wanted to include in the migration anyway.

  1. Directly copy the entire Git repository from Windows to Linux

    • Make sure to copy the entire Git repository, including the .git folder
    • At this point, when I ran git status on Linux, none of the files in the repository were being tracked

  2. Run find . -type f -print0 | xargs -0 dos2unix on the repository on Linux.

    • This will convert all the line endings from Windows format (CRLF) to Linux format (LF).
    • Make sure to include the .git folder when you run this command

  3. Run git add .

    • This will allow Git to track all files again. Usually, the repository is bugged and will show all files as being untracked when you first copy it to Linux.

  4. Run git restore --staged .

    • This is the final step. It will restore the Git repository to the exact status you left it in on Windows. When you do a Git add in the step above, it adds every file that's not ignored in file .gitignore. However, that means that some uncommitted files or uncommitted changes will also be added. By running a Git restore, you untrack these changes and bring the repo back to its original state.

That's all you need to do to migrate a Git repository from Windows to Linux!

Q: How do I run npx bddgen? A:

npx bddgen is something you call to create spec files that Playwright will understand. But... you need to use the playwright-bdd plugin, not the cucumber plugin. You either use Cucumber OR playwright-bdd. playwright-bdd is the better option, because it can make full use of the playwright test runner capabilities, whereas cucumber is limited to well, cucumber.

Q: computing partial area under a curve at specified intervals A:

You need to interpolate first your dataset in order to evaluate missing points. Then you can rely on integrate.quad to make your integration by intervals. I leave here a MCVE:

MCVE

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy import interpolate, integrate

x = np.array([0, 1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.3, 5.0, 6.0, 7.0, 8.0, 9.0, 10, 12, 12.5, 12.7, 13, 14.5, 15, 15.5, 16, 16.5])
y = np.array([0, -0.44, -0.83, -0.91, -1.10, -1.16, -1.00, -1.02, -1.05, -1.0, -0.94, - 0.89, -1, -1.39, -1.44, -1.88, -1.9, -1.94, -2.03, -1.9])

interpolator = interpolate.interp1d(x, y, kind="linear")

bounds = np.array([0, 5, 10, 15])
results = []
for xmin, xmax in zip(bounds[:-1], bounds[1:]):
    I, sI = integrate.quad(interpolator, xmin, xmax)
    results.append({
        "xmin": xmin,
        "xmax": xmax,
        "I": I,
        "sI": sI
    })

The results look like:

#    xmin  xmax       I            sI
# 0     0     5 -3.8225  5.585144e-08
# 1     5    10 -5.1200  5.684342e-15
# 2    10    15 -6.4010  6.011592e-08

Q: "Access to the path is denied" when attempting to redirect output to a file A:

I'm not sure how I could not have access to create a file in a directory on my own machine.

Users do NOT have write access to the entire file system by default, and haven't since at least Windows 2000 and when people first started using NTFS in Windows XP.

In fact, by default, other than a few special cases like the Windows Temp folder, the only place standard users have write access is within their own profile folder.

This is why applications are supposed to use %APPDATA% rather than Program Files for saving preferences now.
